lesson.title: Two Machines, One Job: Inside Photosystems I and II
lesson.summary: Photosystems I and II are pigment protein complexes that funnel absorbed light energy to a reaction center chlorophyll, exciting an electron that begins the light dependent reactions.
lesson.body:
Absorbing a photon is only the first step; that captured energy has to be funneled somewhere useful before it dissipates. Photosynthetic organisms solve this by organizing hundreds of chlorophyll and carotenoid molecules into large pigment protein complexes called photosystems, embedded in the thylakoid membrane. Each photosystem consists of an antenna complex, a cluster of pigment molecules whose job is purely to absorb photons and pass the resulting energy along, surrounding a special pair of chlorophyll a molecules at the reaction center, where the energy is finally put to chemical use.

When a photon strikes any pigment in the antenna complex, its energy is not converted into an electrical signal right away. Instead, the excitation energy hops from pigment to pigment through direct resonance transfer between neighboring molecules, somewhat like a message passed hand to hand, losing a small amount of energy at each step until it reaches the reaction center. Only at the reaction center does something chemically permanent happen: the reaction center chlorophyll absorbs the arriving energy, an electron is boosted to a higher energy level, and that excited electron is captured by a primary electron acceptor molecule, beginning true electron transport rather than simple energy transfer.

Plants and algae use two distinct photosystems, distinguished by the precise absorption peak of their reaction center chlorophyll, a shift caused by each reaction center's unique surrounding protein environment. Photosystem II has a reaction center called P680, absorbing best around six hundred eighty nanometers, while Photosystem I has a reaction center called P700, absorbing best around seven hundred nanometers. Despite the numbering, which reflects the order the two were discovered rather than the order they act, Photosystem II operates first in the normal flow of electrons through the light dependent reactions.

Photosystem II's reaction center, once it loses an electron to the primary acceptor, becomes a powerfully oxidizing molecule that pulls replacement electrons from water, splitting it apart in the process covered in the next concept. The electron that left Photosystem II eventually travels down an electron transport chain to Photosystem I, where a second photon absorption re-energizes it before it is ultimately used to help reduce NADP+ to NADPH. Both photosystems are therefore required in sequence, each contributing one boost of light energy to the same electron on its journey.

This two step, two photosystem arrangement lets plants extract more usable energy from sunlight than a single photosystem could manage alone, since each photosystem only needs to boost an electron partway rather than all the way from water's very low energy level to NADPH's very high one. How these pieces, antenna pigments, reaction centers, and the electron transport chain connecting them, work together as a complete system is the subject of the light dependent reactions covered next.
